name: Dominica
summary_text: On 22 April 2024 the High Court of Justice in Roseau held that sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act were unconstitutional insofar as they criminalised consensual same-sex activity between adults. Reporting on 23 and 24 April 2024 recorded the outcome as decriminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct between adults in Dominica, in a case brought by a gay man living in Dominica.  The court ordered a reading-down rather than a full repeal. Section 14(2) is to be read as exempting private consensual sexual acts between adult persons who consent, and section 16(1)(b) is to be read as exempting private consensual adult acts from the 10-year penalty for buggery.  The prior regime was broad. It criminalised male same-sex sexual activity and female same-sex sexual activity, as well as anal intercourse between persons of the opposite sex. Under the Sexual Offences Act 1998 as amended in 2016, section 14 on gross indecency provided 12 years imprisonment where the complainant was 16 or older, and 14 years for a first offence and 20 years for a subsequent offence where the complainant was under 16, with an exemption only for private consensual adult male-female acts. Section 16 on buggery provided 25 years where committed by an adult on a minor, 10 years where committed by an adult on another adult, 5 years where committed by a minor, and 4 years for attempt or assault with intent to commit buggery, with judicial discretion to order admission to a psychiatric hospital for treatment.  Enforcement before the ruling included custodial and medical penalties. Between 1995 and 2000 there were 35 arrests for buggery resulting in fines and prison sentences of up to 10 years, with some persons sent to psychiatric hospitals for treatment. In 2001, 15 women were sentenced to five years imprisonment for gross indecency and 10 men were sentenced to five years for engaging in gross indecency with persons of the same sex. In 2014 the Prime Minister stated that Dominica did not enforce the law against homosexual activity at least in private homes and had no plans to do so.  Dominica provides no recognition to same-sex unions as marriage or civil unions. No law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.  Protection gaps are documented in police response. The gay man who filed suit in July 2019 challenging the 10-year and 12-year provisions reported that police refused to investigate a vicious home attack and reported physical and sexual assaults because gay people were considered criminals under Dominican law. More generally, reports to police by victims are reported as not taken seriously, with victims sometimes ridiculed.  Violence and intimidation linked to perceived sexual orientation are reported. Sources describe suspected hate crimes against individuals believed to be homosexuals, vandalism against property of openly gay persons, and use in disputes of derogatory terms such as buggerman or battyman to refer to effeminate men. As an example of lethal violence within that pattern, Clement James of Portsmouth was stabbed to death in 2010 after being accused of watching his male assailant in a public place. The accused, Davis St Jean, was reported to preach in the street about killing gay people and to have said all battie boi must dead before the stabbing.  Hostility toward gay visitors has been expressed publicly. In 2009 the president of the Evangelical Association, Bill Daniel, stated that the government should ensure gay tourists do not come to the island and conduct themselves in any immoral way, in a context of association protests against gay cruises visiting the island and against promotion of Dominica as a gay tourist destination.

name: Denmark
summary_text: Denmark permits legal gender recognition by self-declaration since 1 September 2014. A person over 18 changes registered sex by stating the wish and completing a six-month reflection period, without medical evaluation, psychiatric diagnosis, surgery or sterilization. Parliament adopted that removal of diagnosis and surgery requirements in June 2014 by 59 votes to 52.  Danish passports are issued with male, female and X sex descriptors, so a non-binary holder can carry a travel document that records neither male nor female.  Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is prohibited. The Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment and services. The 1996 Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market lists sexual orientation, and a 2015 court ruling in a claim by a transgender woman against a former employer held that gender identity or expression is covered. Workplace protection on gender identity is recorded as in place since 2015, with fair-housing protection on gender identity recorded throughout the period, and complaints are considered by the Board of Equal Treatment established under the 2008 Act.  Additional penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation have applied since 2004 amendments to the Penal Code. The sources do not record the hate-crime penalty provision as expressly covering gender identity or expression.  Freedom from arbitrary arrest on grounds of gender identity is recorded as affirmed in every year from 2011 to 2024.  Same-sex marriage has been legal since 15 June 2012, including marriage in the Church of Denmark, following registered partnership since 1 October 1989. A visitor travelling with a same-sex spouse is therefore travelling under a gender-neutral marriage law.  On 10 September 2024 the Supreme Court held that placement of a trans inmate to serve in a men’s prison department is not a violation of human rights. That ruling is the leading Danish authority on trans placement in custody and indicates the placement risk in detention.  The UN Committee against Torture in its 8th periodic review found that some trans people, QTIBIPOC people and migrants reported denial of access to spaces and services and threats. The Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT+ barometer records that 38 percent of homosexual and bisexual respondents report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance, and that hate speech targeting sexual orientation, gender identity or expression or sex characteristics recurs annually.  In the period covered by the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, a migrant trans woman was murdered in July in a hotel room in Copenhagen.  Access to gender-affirming care in Denmark is gatekept and slow. Patients seeking hormone therapy report being required to present in ways reflecting stereotypical gender roles, with trans men describing a need to give male-coded answers, after several psychological sessions. Recorded adult waits are generally 11 to 16 months for hormone therapy and 4 to 6 years for bottom surgery, which leads many trans adults to seek care abroad. A visitor should not expect timely access to hormones or surgery in country.  There is no ban on conversion therapy. A bill was revived in August 2026, but no prohibition was in force in the sources.  In February 2013 a Guatemalan trans woman, Fernanda Milan, became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark on grounds of persecution for gender identity and trans activism, citing police attacks and threats. She was initially refused, was placed in a facility for men where she was sexually assaulted several times, and authorities reopened the case when she established that return would endanger her life.
